title: How to Choose an Orthopaedic Dog Bed
seo_title: Best Orthopaedic Dog Bed UK: How to Choose | PawLunova
seo_description: Down, up, turn, down again, then the tiles by morning? How to choose the best orthopaedic dog bed in the UK: foam, depth, entry, liners. Start here.
body_html:
Choosing the best orthopaedic dog bed usually starts with something you have already seen. They lie down, get up a minute later, turn, and lie down again on the other side. They stand over the bed for a second before stepping in, as if working out the angle. Or you come into the kitchen first thing and find them on the tiles, with a perfectly good-looking bed sitting empty in the corner.

None of that is a dog being fussy. It is a dog telling you that the surface under them has stopped doing its job, or that getting onto it has started to cost something. This guide, written for UK homes, covers the physical things to check for both, and is straight with you about what a bed can and cannot do.

What “orthopaedic” should actually mean

On a dog bed, orthopaedic (or orthopedic, as American listings spell it) is a description, not a test the bed has passed. So look past the word and check for three physical things instead.

  • A foam core that holds its shape. Loose filling is cheap, and under a dog it drifts away from the heaviest points and packs into ridges. Foam keeps an even surface under the hip and shoulder, night after night.
  • Enough depth for their weight. A heavy dog on a thin layer is, in effect, lying on the floor through some fabric.
  • A way in they can manage. Deep walls feel cosy to a young dog. To a stiff one they are a climb, and beds that need climbing quietly stop being used.

If a bed sold as orthopaedic will not tell you what its core is made of, how deep it is and how a dog gets onto it, that is your answer.

Memory foam, egg-crate foam or fibre?

  • Memory foam moulds slowly around a hip or shoulder instead of pushing back at one point. You will find it as an open, 10cm-deep mattress in Buttermere, as crumb in Chatsworth, and with gel through it in Ennerdale.
  • Egg-crate foam is cut into peaks and hollows. It spreads weight, resists packing flat and feels livelier underfoot. Nocturne, Newlands, Easedale and Scafell use it.
  • Layered foam stacks the two: memory foam to contour on top, profiled or firmer foam beneath so heavier dogs are less likely to sink through to the floor. Martindale, Rosthwaite and Watendlath work this way.
  • Fibre fill is soft and cosy, and some dogs love it. It is not support: it drifts away from the heaviest points and flattens, which is why our fibre-filled nests are sold for softness.

For the longer version, including how to spot foam that has given up, read what's inside our beds.

Depth, sides and the way in

Depth matters more as weight goes up, because a heavy dog compresses a thin layer until the floor is doing the supporting. When you compare beds, check what a depth figure is measuring. On an open mattress it is the cushioning itself: Buttermere is 10cm of memory foam, Ennerdale 24cm of gel memory foam. On a bolstered bed a listed depth can include the walls, so ask about the base if it is not clear.

Deeper is not automatically kinder, though. Every centimetre of mattress is also a centimetre of step. For a big dog who still moves well, depth is worth having. For a small dog with stiff back legs, a lower bed they can walk onto may get more use.

Then look at how they get in. Walls give a leaning dog something to press into, and most dogs like at least one edge. The question is whether they have to climb it. Shapes that keep an edge without the climb:

  • An open front with bolsters on three sides: Melbreak, Staveley, Martindale and Rosthwaite.
  • A lowered front inside a four-sided surround, for dogs who want walls all round: Newlands, Easedale and Burnmoor.
  • An open corner, chaise-style: Braithwaite, for small and medium dogs.
  • A low profile: the oval Coniston, close to the floor with a chin-height rim.
  • No walls at all: the open mattresses, which they can step onto from any side.

On wooden or tiled floors, check for a non-slip base too. A dog who pushes off the edge to stand needs the bed to stay where it is. Martindale, Rosthwaite, Newlands, Easedale and Nocturne all have one, and Helvellyn uses silicone dots.

Getting the size right

Nose to base of tail, lying on their side, plus 15 to 20cm: that is the smallest sleeping area worth buying. Remember that a bolstered bed's listed size is usually the outside, and the walls take their share. Our Chatsworth Large is 70 × 55cm outside but 50 × 45cm to lie on. Between two sizes, size up. The dog bed size guide has a breed table and the full method.

Covers, liners and keeping it clean

Foam should never go in the washing machine or be soaked, so an orthopaedic bed lives or dies by its cover and by what sits between the cover and the core. Look for two things. A cover that comes off without a fight, because a cover that is hard to refit does not get washed; Melbreak's opens on three sides for exactly that reason. And a waterproof liner between cover and foam, so a wet coat or one bad night stays out of the core. Coniston, Borrowdale, Helvellyn, Staveley, Newlands, Easedale, Scafell and Wastwater all have one.

Red flags when comparing orthopaedic dog beds

  • The filling is not named. If a listing does not say what the core is, ask before you buy.
  • Only outside dimensions on a bed with thick walls, so you cannot tell how much of it your dog can lie on.
  • Nothing to protect the foam: a cover that does not come off, and nothing between it and the core.
  • Promises about pain. A bed can make lying down and getting up easier. It is not a medical product, and a listing that says otherwise is telling you something about the seller.
  • A trial you would never use. If sending a bed back means paying to post something the size of a mattress, check who arranges and pays for the collection.

The best orthopaedic dog bed for your dog: where to start

Rather than a ranking, here is a starting point for some common situations.

  • A big dog who sleeps flat out: Ambleside, foam right out to the edges and up to 140 × 100cm, or Wastwater, whose headrest is shaped into the foam itself.
  • A dog who has started pausing at the edge: Coniston's low oval, or Newlands' lowered front if they still want walls. Our guide to helping an older dog sleep well covers where to put the bed and when to ask your vet.
  • A heavy or giant breed: Mardale, Longsleddale or Burnmoor at 132 × 104cm, or Ennerdale's 24cm of gel memory foam.
  • Occasional accidents: any bed with a waterproof liner, such as Borrowdale, which also has a border on all four sides.
  • A first proper foam bed on a budget: Chatsworth, crumb memory foam with bolster walls, in Small, Medium and Large.

All of these are in our orthopaedic dog beds collection.

A bed is comfort, not a treatment

Everything above is about the surface your dog rests on. It is not medical advice. If your dog is stiff, sore, slowing down quickly or struggling to get up, your vet is the person to see, and they can tell you what kind of resting surface suits your dog's joints. Keep them in the loop as things change.

Try it at home for 100 nights

Every orthopaedic dog bed in our range comes with a 100-night trial from delivery, so the real test happens where it should: on your floor, with your dog. If it is not right, we arrange free UK mainland collection and a full refund. One trial per household; damage and other exclusions apply. Many of the memory foam beds also carry a 5-year no-flatten guarantee on the foam core, under normal domestic use and subject to the guarantee terms; each product page says whether it applies. Standard UK delivery is free on orders over £40.

Orthopaedic dog bed questions

Does a young dog need an orthopaedic bed?

Need, no. But a bed that keeps its shape is worth having at any age, especially for big, heavy breeds who press a lot of weight into a few points. A bed that keeps its shape is one you are not replacing every spring.

How firm should an orthopaedic dog bed be?

Firm enough that hips and shoulders never reach the floor, soft enough that they sink in a little. Push down with a flat hand where the hip would go: you want to feel the foam take the weight and push back, not the floorboards.

How long should an orthopaedic dog bed last?

Until the foam stops recovering. When a dip is still there in the morning, or you can feel the floor through the sleeping area, it has stopped doing its job. Where one of our beds carries the 5-year no-flatten guarantee, the product page says so, and the guarantee terms explain what is covered; cover wear and pet damage are not included.
